title: Surge traffic matrix + warmup experiment log
content:
Meeting: Surge traffic matrix and warmup experiment sync
Date: 2029-02-06
Attendees: Arjun (owner), Maya, Liam, Nora, SRE oncall (Jess), Solutions (Ravi)

1) Purpose / high-level objective
- We want an operationally simple warmup approach that meaningfully reduces cold-start tail latency for short chat sessions (median tokens per request ~45) during sudden regional surges, without materially increasing steady-state cost.
- This document captures the experiment design, early observations from the lab run (2029-02-05), and an action plan for the next two-week sprint.

2) Background context
- Recent customer incident (INFRA-1428) showed 99th percentile latency spikes in eu-west1 when a marketing event triggered a sudden QPS jump (~6x baseline) for 8 minutes.
- Current prewarming policy uses a per-region warm pool sized by 99th percentile QPS over 24h with conservative buffer; it reduces average cold-starts but doesn't address short, high-amplitude bursts.

3) Experiment hypothesis
- Hypothesis A: A lightweight prefix-KV prefetch (30s of synthetic 'priming' tokens per worker on allocation) will reduce 95/99 p95/p99 token-latency on first live request by >40% during surge windows.
- Hypothesis B: A short-lived regional short-warm pool (workers that stay 'semi-warm' for 3 minutes with reduced memory footprint) can cover 60% of microbursts with <6% steady-state cost increase if coupled with request-based on-demand promotion.

4) Lab run summary (2029-02-05, noisy-lab cluster)
- Setup: 3 region mocks (us-west2, eu-west1, ap-south1), model: rwd-13b-q4f, baseline workers: 32 per region, surge pattern: 0 -> 6x baseline over 20s, hold 4 minutes, decay 30s.
- Warmup variants tested (A/B/C):
  A) No warmup (baseline)
  B) KV-prefetch 30s (single synthetic request per worker at allocation)
  C) Short-warm pool (3m TTL, lightweight memory foot-print) + on-demand promotion
- Observables captured: first-request p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), tokens/sec initial slope, eviction spikes, GPU util curves, and estimated cost delta per minute.

5) Key observations (quantitative)
- Baseline (A): first-request p99 = 2,340 ms; p95 = 1,220 ms; median small.
- KV-prefetch (B): p99 = 1,420 ms (39% reduction), p95 = 760 ms (38% reduction). Cold token throughput ramp improved 2.2x in first 10s. CPU sidecar signals increased ~6% during priming windows.
- Short-warm (C): p99 = 1,200 ms (49% reduction vs baseline), p95 = 680 ms (44% reduction). Effective coverage of microbursts: ~58% of synthetic bursts served by warm pool workers without allocation during peak.
- Cost impact (lab estimate): B -> ~+3.8% ops cost; C -> ~+5.9% ops cost if warm pools are sized to cover 60% of bursts.
- Side-effects: B increased sidecar memory churn during allocation; C required additional scheduler hooks to avoid aggressive eviction during warm TTL.

6) Operational tradeoffs / notes
- KV-prefetch is simpler to implement in runtime (single hook on allocation) and has predictable small CPU/memory overhead per allocation. Less scheduler changes required.
- Short-warm pool requires new lifecycle states and TTL enforcement plus accounting for memory/gpu occupancy; more invasive to scheduler but better coverage for sustained microbursts.
- Both approaches interact with our eviction heuristics; need to ensure the scheduler differentiates between warm-pool and active-serving workers to avoid preemption thrash.

7) Pending questions / unknowns
- How will these numbers vary for larger models (rwd-70b) and quantization variants? Early sims show B scales linearly in CPU overhead but C's memory footprint grows non-linearly. Need a smoke test on 70b-sim nodes.
- How do these strategies affect audit/compliance traces (private deployments)? Warm pools holding cached prefixes may leak traceable prompt tokens—need security review (cc: security team).
- Impact on Dedicated customers with pinned capacity: warm pools may underutilize reserved GPUs if not charged to tenant quotas. Need billing/product input.

8) Immediate actions (owners + ETA)
- A1: Run a 70b-sim lab run for variant B and C (Liam) — ETA 2029-02-09.
- A2: Short design doc for scheduler state machine for short-warm pool (Maya) — ETA 2029-02-12.
- A3: Security review ticket for warm cache content (Arjun) — create INFRA-1436 — ETA 2029-02-08.
- A4: Cost model update: run cost simulator for per-minute warm pool sizing across regions (Nora + Finance) — ETA 2029-02-14.
- A5: Add a canary pipeline step to runtime CI that flips KV-prefetch flag for a small subset of traffic in eu-west1 (SRE) — ETA 2029-02-15.

9) Notes from discussion
- Solutions recommended prioritizing minimal-impact change first (KV-prefetch) and only add short-warm pool if the priming hook fails to meet 99th percentile SLOs at scale.
- SRE emphasized observability: add a new metric warm_pool_hit_ratio and priming_cpu_seconds_per_alloc. Instrumentation ticket created (INFRA-1437).
- Maya flagged a corner case where warm pool + autoscaler burst policy could lead to double-counting available capacity; scheduler change must expose 'reserved_for_warm' metric to autoscaler.

10) Risk register (short bullets)
- Risk: Warm caches may contain sensitive prefixes — Mitigation: encrypt in-memory caches and rotate/limit prefix content.
- Risk: Warm pools cause fragmentation in low-util regions — Mitigation: region-specific policy and lower TTL thresholds for edge regions.
- Risk: Cost overshoot if warm pools left running — Mitigation: strict TTL + automatic drain if rolling 5m utilization < 30%.

11) Next steps & meeting cadence
- Weekly sync on Wednesdays 10:00am PT; weekly readout in infra standup on Fridays for cross-team visibility.
- Review of Liam's 70b-sim run and Maya's scheduler doc scheduled for 2029-02-13 design review.

12) Attachments / artifacts referenced in meeting
- Lab logs (s3://lab-logs/surge-warmup/2029-02-05/)
- Synthetic traffic generator config: GH PR #3345 (runtime)
- Jira tickets: INFRA-1428 (incident), INFRA-1436 (security review), INFRA-1437 (metrics)

Open questions for the group:
- Product: are we comfortable with a small steady-state cost delta to improve 99p during marketing-driven microbursts? (cc: @product-hosted-api)
- Sales/Account teams: any Dedicated customers we should pilot the feature with to jointly tune TTL/chargeback?

-- end of notes --

Quick snapshot for search: warmup experiment, KV-prefetch, short-warm pool, microburst coverage, p99 reductions, cost delta estimates.
